reason: Sepals can be dark or dusky. Some examples describe lobe midribs, which is a minor misattachment.
Wrong reading. 'Acute' is the shape of a tip, not sharpness as an attribute. A rule should map acute, acuminate and the like to apex shape terms.
Stolons can be woody or lignified, and the examples show this.
Peristome teeth spread or do not spread when dry. This is a real moss character.
'Surrounded by' or 'concealed by' is a relation to another part (bracts or sheaths), not a quality of the inflorescence. It needs a relation pattern.
Stigmas and stigma heads can be terete. The examples are correct.
A corolla can be pendent, meaning drooping. Some examples are about other parts (utricle, lobes).
Wrong reading. 'Persistent' in the examples refers to bases or indument, not to the whole plant being non-deciduous. A rule would need to send persistence to the named part.
The only example is the single word 'columnar', with no part named. A rule would need the part or a context word to tell a column-like anther from a column-like filament or staminal column.
The bearer is floral corona. Examples are just 'laminar' from one flora. A corona can be sheet-like, but the part is not shown. A rule would need the part named.
Pinnae can be narrow. A few examples refer to other parts (apex) or to comparisons.
Bracteoles can be elongated, and the examples show this.
Wrong part. 'Woody crown' describes the base of a perennial herb, not a tree crown. A rule would need to map crown on herbs to a different part.
Tepals can be papery or chartaceous.
Wrong part. 'Terete' belongs to the stem or axis, and 'junciforme' is a habit. It is not a quality of the whole plant.
Mericarps can be obovate. The examples are correct.
Wrong reading. The examples describe a fringed membrane surrounding another structure, not the secretory tissue itself.
A hypanthium can be crateriform or bowl-shaped. This is common in botany.
Achenes can be mottled in colour.
The bract abaxial surface can be scabrous or tuberculate. The texture attribute is generic, so values would be better, but the pair is meaningful.
Achenes can be emarginate at the apex or base. Some examples name the apex or base as the part.
A perigynium can be inflated or not. This is a Carex character.
Wrong part. The examples are about conspicuous sutures or beaks, not the perigynium itself.
A leaf blade base can be folded. The examples are correct.
A blade base can be flat. The examples are correct.
A stem can be reflexed, but the examples seem to be about parts on the stem (hairs, branches) or a later stage. A rule would need to find the part that is reflexed.
A pericarp can be papery or papyraceous.
A leaf collar has a colour (stramineous, brown, white).
A leaf blade can be perfoliate. The examples are correct.
An ochrea can have an oblique mouth or margin. Some examples name the apex or margin.
Pedicels can be conspicuous or not.
Thorns or spines can be dark, or darker in the centre or at the tip.
Areoles are woolly or lanate in cacti. The examples are correct.
Areoles can be conspicuous or not. Some examples are about glands on the areole.
Bracteoles can be herbaceous, meaning leaf-like in texture.
Leaf lobes can be inconspicuous or indistinct.
Thorns or spines can be soft.
The examples are about the midvein or lateral veins on the valve, not the valve. A rule would need to send the quality to the vein.
Most examples are about sharp teeth, not the margin. A real sharp margin (cutting edge) exists. A rule would need to tell tooth sharpness from margin sharpness.
Wrong reading. 'Short-stalked' describes the stalk of the pinnule, not the pinnule length. It needs a stalk or petiolule bearer.
Sepals have a colour.
A short shoot can be thick or slender, and the examples give thickness.
A keel can be dentate or denticulate.
Cauline leaves can be sessile or petiolate. The attribute is generic, but the pair is meaningful.
The attribute is too generic. The examples mix a leaf shape (obreniform) with a capsule shape (urceolate). A rule would need to map urceolate to a specific value and drop leaf-shape words.
Branches can be square in cross-section. This is common in some families.
Spikelets can be keeled, but the examples may refer to glumes or margins. A rule would need to find which part carries the keel.
A perianth can bear small spines (spinulose), for example on bristles or margins.
A spathe can be ovoid or ellipsoid.
The examples are fractions of exsertion from one flora. It is not clear that the sporophyll is the exserted part and not the sporangium. A rule would need the part named.
An inflorescence axis can be glandular.
The examples count teeth, not lobes. A count of teeth on an involucre needs a tooth bearer. A rule would need to decide whether lobes and teeth are the same here.
Wrong part. 'Margins entire' describes a leaf or organ margin, not a portion of secretory tissue.
A midvein can be translucent.
Involucral bracts, or their margins, can be involute.
Leaves can be crowded or not crowded.
A corolla lip can be glandular. Some examples describe glands on its inner surface or margin.
Tubercles can be narrow.
Areoles have a diameter.
A hypanthium can be radially symmetric. Only one flora gives examples.
